text: {"master_id": "bert-ligon", "work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "usage_notes": [{"chord_quality": "min7", "function_role": "ii-in-major-harmonic-family", "narrative": "Ligon places the ii chord (minor seventh) as the initiating member of the ii-V-I progression, and identifies its third as the single most harmonically specific melodic target. F reveals the minor quality of the chord and is the best choice for harmonically specific counterpoint over the D in the bass; playing just the F over D in the bass sounds like a complete minor chord even though only two notes are being played. The root is omitted because the bass covers it, opening eleven pitch choices while preserving harmonic clarity. Chapter 2, p. 5.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:guide-tone-pair", "bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:root-omission"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 2 p.5"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "min7", "function_role": "ii-in-major-seventh-as-pointer", "narrative": "The seventh of the ii chord is the 'restless pointer' that drives melodic momentum. Sevenths resolve downward to the third of the following chord. For the ii min7, the seventh must land on a metrically significant beat, positioned later in the line than the third, so that its downward resolution to the V7's third is perceptible as directed motion. Chapter 2, p. 5-6.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:seventh-to-third-resolution", "bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:third-placement-priority"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 2 p.5-6"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "min7", "function_role": "ii-in-major-outline-1-shell", "narrative": "Over the ii min7, Outline No. 1 begins on beat one with the third, descends stepwise through the chord, and delivers the seventh on beat four as the pointer into the V7. Placing the third on beat one and waiting for beat four to play the seventh leaves only two beats to fill, creating a walking quarter-note melody line to counter the walking bass line. Chapter 2, p. 6.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:outline-1"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 2 p.6; chapter 4 p.18"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "min7", "function_role": "ii-in-major-outline-2-ascending-arpeggio", "narrative": "Outline No. 2 treats the ii min7 as an ascending arpeggio 1-3-5-7, where the seventh functions as the restless tone that resolves to the third of the V7 chord. The canonical form begins on the root of the ii chord and spells the arpeggio to the seventh. Fragments that omit the root are fully valid because the bass covers the root. Chapter 2 p. 8; Chapter 5 p. 60, 63.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:outline-2", "bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:outline-fragmentation"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 2 p.8"}, {"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 5 p.60"}, {"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 5 p.63"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "min7", "function_role": "ii-in-major-outline-3-descending-arpeggio", "narrative": "Outline No. 3 descends the ii min7 as 5-3-1, then adds the seventh below as a pointer tone. The seventh usually occurs on the upbeat; the target third on the strong downbeat. The leap from the third of the ii to the flat-nine of the V creates compound melody as a byproduct. Chapter 2 p. 9; Chapter 6 p. 66.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:outline-3", "bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:compound-melody-split"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 2 p.9"}, {"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 6 p.66"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "min7", "function_role": "ii-in-major-punch-line-rule", "narrative": "When using Outline No. 2 over a ii min7, the sixth scale degree (the tone that will become the third of the following V7) must be reserved for the V7 chord and not used as a passing tone on the ii. This tone is the punch line, the denouement of the story, not given away ahead of time as a passing tone. Early arrival of the target tone collapses the harmonic tension the outline is designed to build. Chapter 5 p. 54.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:punch-line-rule"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 5 p.54"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "min7", "function_role": "ii-in-major-punch-line-rule-exception", "narrative": "The punch line rule (reserving the target note for the V7) may be broken when the line extends to the ninth of the ii chord, reducing the premature arrival's disruptive effect. The extension contextualizes the early target as an inner passing tone rather than a harmonic spoiler. Chapter 5 p. 58.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:punch-line-rule"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 5 p.58"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "V7-in-major-harmonic-family", "narrative": "Ligon treats the dominant seventh as the resolution target for the ii chord's seventh-as-pointer: the V7's third is the single most important arrival note in the ii-V-I progression. The third of V7 is the downbeat destination that sounds at rest after the restless seventh of ii. All three outlines converge on this arrival point as their primary harmonic goal. Chapter 2 p. 5-6.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:seventh-to-third-resolution"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 2 p.5-6"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "V7-in-major-parallel-minor-color-tones", "narrative": "Over any dominant seventh functioning as V7 in major, Ligon prescribes borrowing the flat-9, sharp-9, and flat-13 from the parallel minor key. Over G7, the dominant of C major, jazz musicians often use A-flat (b9), B-flat (#9) and E-flat (b13) from the parallel key of C minor. These borrowed tones have greater downward pull than their diatonic counterparts. Chapter 3 p. 16.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:parallel-minor-borrowing"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 3 p.16"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "V7-in-major-cesh-chromatic-elaboration", "narrative": "C.E.S.H. (Chromatic Elaboration of Static Harmony) is the characteristic chromatic device applied across the ii-V progression, superimposing a descending chromatic line from the root of the ii down to the third of the V7. In the key of C (D minor-G7), the movement is D-C#-C-B. All three outlines support C.E.S.H., and Outline No. 3 has a special affinity for it. Chapter 3 p. 15; Chapter 4 p. 39; Chapter 6 p. 68.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:cesh-chromatic-elaboration"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 3 p.15"}, {"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 4 p.39"}, {"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 6 p.68"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "V7-in-major-compound-melody-flat-nine-leap", "narrative": "The signature Outline No. 3 move over the V7 is the leap from the third to the flat-nine, which splits the line into a primary melody and a counter-melody. The first and last four notes sound like the primary melody; the middle notes sound like a secondary answer or counter melody. This is the idiomatic octave-displacement move specific to the V7 within Outline No. 3. Chapter 6 p. 66.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:compound-melody-split", "bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:octave-displacement"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 6 p.66"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "V7-in-major-target-tone-rhythmic-placement", "narrative": "Chromatic non-chord tones over the V7 are licensed only when target tones (the third and seventh of the dominant) land on metrically strong beats. All twelve chromatic pitches may be used yet harmonically clear; not random chromaticism. Target notes occur in rhythmically significant spots, non-harmonic chromatic notes resolve when and where expected. Chapter 4 p. 43; Chapter 6 p. 74.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:target-on-strong-beat"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 4 p.43"}, {"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 6 p.74"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "V7-in-major-ascending-scale-skips-target", "narrative": "When an ascending scalar passage approaches an upcoming target note on the V7, the scale must skip the target pitch rather than include it as a passing tone. Premature scalar arrival at the target weakens its harmonic impact on the strong beat. Chapter 4 p. 32.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:target-on-strong-beat"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 4 p.32"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "V7-in-major-octave-displacement-3rd-to-9th", "narrative": "The signature octave displacement move over V7 replaces a descending step from the third to the second with an ascending seventh leap from the third up to the ninth or flat-ninth. The leap must occur after the guide tone, from downbeat to upbeat, and never crosses the barline. Chapter 3 p. 14.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:octave-displacement"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 3 p.14"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "V7-in-major-encircling-target", "narrative": "The third of the V7 may be approached by encirclement - diatonic upper neighbor tone followed by chromatic lower neighbor tone, or the reverse - to create tension and momentary ambiguity before resolution. The common practice from Mozart to Charlie Parker uses the diatonic UNT and the chromatic LNT. Chapter 5 p. 52; Chapter 3 p. 11.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:encircling-target", "bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:unt-lnt-convention"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 5 p.52"}, {"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 3 p.11"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "min7b5", "function_role": "ii-in-minor-outline-applicability", "narrative": "Ligon explicitly extends all three outlines to the minor ii-V context, treating the half-diminished chord as a direct functional equivalent of the diatonic ii min7 in terms of outline applicability. All the outlines work as well for half-diminished/V7 in minor as they do in major. The same target-tone logic applies: third of half-dim is the opening melodic goal; its seventh resolves to the third of the V7. Chapter 5 p. 52.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:universal-fifth-motion-applicability"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 5 p.52"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7b9", "function_role": "V7-in-minor-parallel-minor-borrowing", "narrative": "Over the dominant V7 in a minor ii-V-i context, Ligon's parallel-minor borrowing rule carries the same force as in major: the flat-9, sharp-9, and flat-13 are drawn from the parallel minor and prescribed as melodic color tones that resolve with greater downward pull than their diatonic counterparts. Because the minor ii-V already exists in a minor-key harmonic environment, the borrowed tones are particularly idiomatic. Chapter 3 p. 16.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:parallel-minor-borrowing"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 3 p.16"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "sus4", "function_role": "dominant-sus-ii-V-equivalence", "narrative": "Ligon teaches that dominant sus4 voicings are interchangeable with ii-V7 voicings for outline purposes. Since this sound is essentially the ii and V7 chord together, any of the outlines will work for this harmony. A sus chord is treated not as a separate harmonic category but as a composite of ii and V7 stacked, meaning all three outlines and their embellishment devices apply without modification. Chapter 6 p. 65.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:universal-fifth-motion-applicability"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 6 p.65"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "min7", "function_role": "modal-ii-bebop-outline-superimposition", "narrative": "Over a modal ii min7 context (e.g., G Dorian), Ligon prescribes superimposing bebop outlines via leading-tone approach to bring harmonic clarity to an otherwise static harmonic environment. The mechanics demonstrated by Cannonball Adderley include approaching chord tones by their leading tones and using encircling motion; outline no.1 can be clearly heard on the downbeats with leading tones added giving the line more of a sawtooth shape. Chapter 8 p. 78.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:bebop-outline-over-modal"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 8 p.78"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "modal-V7-cesh-outline-3-contrast-device", "narrative": "In modal blues contexts, the C.E.S.H. version of Outline No. 3 over the dominant functions as a deliberate contrast device against motivic and blues-inflected playing. Cannonball Adderley uses this C.E.S.H. version of outline no.3 several times in the solo to contrast with his modal, motivic, and down-and-dirty blues playing on this modal blues tune. The outline's harmonic specificity stands out precisely because the surrounding context is harmonically vague. Chapter 8 p. 78.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:bebop-outline-over-modal", "bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:cesh-chromatic-elaboration"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 8 p.78"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "V7-universal-root-motion-by-fifths", "narrative": "Ligon explicitly states that any chord progression with root motion descending by fifths - not only ii-V-I but secondary dominants, back-cycling progressions, blues turnarounds, and standard-tune sequences - is governed by the same three-outline system. Anytime root movement is down in fifths, any of these outlines will work, regardless of chord quality. The quality of the chords does not restrict outline selection; root motion is the controlling factor. Chapter 4 p. 29.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:universal-fifth-motion-applicability"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 4 p.29"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "min7", "function_role": "ii-fragment-omission-policy", "narrative": "Outline fragments that omit chord tones from the ii min7 retain full harmonic clarity as long as the target tones are placed and resolved correctly. Parker's technique demonstrates that the seventh of ii resolving to the third of V7 is a sufficient harmonic kernel even without all chord tones present. Morgan's technique shows the only note missing is the third of the half-diminished ii and the line still follows the outline. These omissions are valid because the root of the chord is covered by the bass. Chapter 7 p. 76-77.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:outline-fragmentation", "bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:root-omission"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 7 p.76"}, {"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 7 p.77"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "V7-stop-and-go-rhythmic-delay", "narrative": "Ligon's answer-key appendix codifies rhythmic delay as a device over V7: stop-and-go rhythms delay the resolution of E7 until beat three; arpeggio on E7 (3-5-7-9). The stop-and-go rhythm withholds the target note arrival beyond its expected metric position, extending the tension of the outline across additional beats. The arpeggio formula 3-5-7-9 is the named chord-tone pattern deployed in this context. Chapter 16 p. 145.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:target-on-strong-beat"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 16 p.145"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "V7-sawtooth-chromatic-leading-tone", "narrative": "The sawtooth embellishment device over V7 combines a leap back to a chord tone with a chromatic leading tone that precedes the target. Leap back to a chord tone creates sawtooth shape, delays resolution of C7; chromatic leading tone (D#) precedes target note (E); leap from third to root of C7. The chromatic leading tone, being a sharped note, follows the upward-tendency rule, pulling directly into the target note on the strong beat. Chapter 16 p. 145; Chapter 3 p. 11.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:chromatic-direction-rule"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 16 p.145"}, {"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 3 p.11"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "V7-neighbor-tone-upper-and-lower-surrounding", "narrative": "The target note on the V7 may be surrounded by both its upper and lower neighbor tones in succession before arrival: target note (A) approached from above (C-Bb-A) and below (G-G#-A). Upper approach is diatonic; lower approach is chromatic, consistent with the UNT/LNT convention. Chapter 16 p. 145.", "source_principle_ids": ["bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:encircling-target", "bert-ligon:connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony:linear-harmony-outline-system:unt-lnt-convention"], "source_work_id": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "references": [{"source": "connecting-chords-with-linear-harmony", "citation": "chapter 16 p.145"}], "provenance": "extracted"}]}
